title: The repayment is made after the market state is update in the `WildcatMarket.repayOutstandingDebt` and `WildcatMarket.repayDelinquentDebt` functions thus putting the borrower at a disadvantage
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L205-L208
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L186-L187
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L179-L180
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L172


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Description:

In the `WildcatMarket.repay` function and the `WildcatMarketWithdrawals.repayAndProcessUnpaidWithdrawalBatches` the `repyament of the borrower` is made before the market state is updated. The natspec comments given for the `repayAndProcessUnpaidWithdrawalBatches` function is as follows:

```solidity
    // Repay before updating state to ensure the paid amount is counted towards
    // any pending or unpaid withdrawals.
```

Hence according to the above natspec comments it is clear that repayment needs to be done prior to market updates since the `repaid amount` can be used to cover for pending or unpaid withdrawals. This is how the protocol is designed to operate.

But the issue is in the `WildcatMarket.repayOutstandingDebt` and `WildcatMarket.repayDelinquentDebt` functions the `market state update` happens `before the funds are repaid` to the market contract. Hence these repaid amounts are not used to cover for the `pending or unpaid withdrawals`. Hence there is a discrepancy in the execution flow of the above different repay mechanisms. 

For certain repayments the transferred amount is not accounted for the immediate repayment towards the pending or unpaid withdrawals. Where as for the other repayments the transferred amount is accounted for the immediate repayment towards the pending or unpaid withdrawals.

## Impact

Let's consider the borrower is in the `deliquent state` for his market. He decides to repay the `deliquent debt` by calling the `WildcatMarket.repayDelinquentDebt` function. Though he repays the `deliquent debt` amount it is not immediately accounted in the contract state since the `market state` update happens prior to the `repayment`. His repayment will only take effect when the `market state` is updated for a later transaction. During this period he could exceed the `deliquent grace period` or `could add additional time on this deliquent grace duration` which is either way disadvantageous to the borrower.

As a result the borrower will have to incur `deliquent interest fee` which he shouldn't have paid in the first place if the `repayment` was done prior to the `market state` update in the `WildcatMarket.repayDelinquentDebt` function.

## Proof of Concept

```solidity
    asset.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount);
    emit_DebtRepaid(msg.sender, amount);

    MarketState memory state = _getUpdatedState();
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L205-L208

```solidity
  function repayDelinquentDebt() external nonReentrant sphereXGuardExternal {
    MarketState memory state = _getUpdatedState();
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L186-L187

```solidity
  function repayOutstandingDebt() external nonReentrant sphereXGuardExternal {
    MarketState memory state = _getUpdatedState();
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L179-L180

```solidity
    asset.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount);
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L172


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Hence it is recommended to ensure that the `repayment` is done prior to the `market state` update in the `WildcatMarket.repayDelinquentDebt` and `WildcatMarket.repayOutstandingDebt` functions. This will ensure that repayment done by the borrower is immediately accounted for the repayment towards the pending or unpaid withdrawals. Thus ensuring the states of the borrower are not adversely affected.



## Assessed type

Other

raw_row.title: Invalid `hooks templates` could be used for market deployments in the `HooksFactory.deployMarket` function

title: Invalid `hooks templates` could be used for market deployments in the `HooksFactory.deployMarket` function
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/HooksFactory.sol#L506-L515
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/HooksFactory.sol#L530-L544


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details

The `HooksFactory.deployMarketAndHooks` function is used to deploy a hooks instance and a new market using the deployed hooks instance. In this function when the `hooks instance is deployed` the following check is performed on the `HooksTemplate` to check whether it `exists`.

```solidity
    HooksTemplate memory templateDetails = _templateDetails[hooksTemplate]; //@audit-info - get the HooksTemplate struct
    if (!templateDetails.exists) {
      revert HooksTemplateNotFound(); 
    }
    hooksInstance = _deployHooksInstance(hooksTemplate, hooksTemplateArgs);
```

The above check ensures that the provided `hooksTemplate` is valid and does exist to be used in the market deployment.

The `HooksFactory.deployMarket` function is also used for the market deployment. But the issue is that the `template details` of the `hooksTemplate` used for the market deployment in this function is not checked for `templateDetails.exists` flag.

## Impact

As a result of the above vulnerability, even when the `templateDetails.exists == false` the market deployment will proceed without any revert, thus enabling invalid `hooks templates` to be used for the market deployments. Hence this vulnerability breaks the intended behavior of the protocol.

## Proof of Concept

```solidity
    HooksTemplate memory templateDetails = _templateDetails[hooksTemplate];
    market = _deployMarket(
      parameters,
      hooksData,
      hooksTemplate,
      templateDetails,
      salt,
      originationFeeAsset,
      originationFeeAmount
    );
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/HooksFactory.sol#L506-L515

```solidity
    HooksTemplate memory templateDetails = _templateDetails[hooksTemplate];
    if (!templateDetails.exists) {
      revert HooksTemplateNotFound();
    }
    hooksInstance = _deployHooksInstance(hooksTemplate, hooksTemplateArgs);
    parameters.hooks = parameters.hooks.setHooksAddress(hooksInstance);
    market = _deployMarket(
      parameters,
      hooksData,
      hooksTemplate,
      templateDetails,
      salt,
      originationFeeAsset,
      originationFeeAmount
    );
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/HooksFactory.sol#L530-L544

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Hence it is recommended to update the `HooksFactory.deployMarket` function to check for the `!templateDetails.exists` flag before the `_deployMarket` is called, and revert the transaction if the `templateDetails.exists == false`. This will ensure that invalid `hooks templates` are not used for the market deployments.



## Assessed type

Other

title: `CREATE2` address collision during deploying of Market  allows draining of market
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/HooksFactory.sol#L426
 https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/HooksFactory.sol#L368


# Vulnerability details

(NOTE: This report is similar to [this past valid report](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-panoptic-findings/issues/482#issuecomment-2096043469). Necessary changes have been made to suit the Wildcard Protocol.)
The attack consists of two parts: Finding a collision, and actually draining the funds in market.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/HooksFactory.sol#L426

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/HooksFactory.sol#L368

**PoC: Finding a collision**
In `HookFactorys::computeMarketAddress`, `CREATE2` salt is user-supplied .
```solidity
//@audit-info : salt is user supplied .
function computeMarketAddress(bytes32 salt) external view override returns (address) {
    return LibStoredInitCode.calculateCreate2Address(ownCreate2Prefix, salt, marketInitCodeHash);
  }
```


 Which is then passed to `LibStoredInitCode::calculateCreate2Address`

```solidity
function calculateCreate2Address(
    uint256 create2Prefix,
    bytes32 salt,
    uint256 initCodeHash
  ) internal pure returns (address create2Address) {
    assembly {
      // Cache the free memory pointer so it can be restored at the end
      let freeMemoryPointer := mload(0x40)

      // Write 0xff + address to bytes 11:32
      mstore(0x00, create2Prefix)

      // Write salt to bytes 32:64
  @>    mstore(0x20, salt)

      // Write initcode hash to bytes 64:96
      mstore(0x40, initCodeHash)

      // Calculate create2 address
  @>    create2Address := and(keccak256(0x0b, 0x55),  0xffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff)

      // Restore the free memory pointer
      mstore(0x40, freeMemoryPointer)
    }
  }
```


Also note that market is deployed as follows using a  user supplied salt 

```
  function _deployMarket(
    DeployMarketInputs memory parameters,
    bytes memory hooksData,
    address hooksTemplate,
    HooksTemplate memory templateDetails,
@>    bytes32 salt,
    address originationFeeAsset,
    uint256 originationFeeAmount
  ) internal returns (address market) {
      // other part of code 
   
@>  LibStoredInitCode.create2WithStoredInitCode(marketInitCodeStorage, salt);

     // other part of code 
```

The address collision an attacker will need to find are:

 - One undeployed Wildcard market address (1).
 - Arbitrary attacker-controlled wallet contract (2).

Both sets of addresses can be brute-force searched because wildcard market address that is to be deployed is computed using  the `initCodeHash` and `salt` which is user supplied and also 


-  By brute-forcing many salt values, we have obtained many different (undeployed) wallet accounts for (1). The user can know the address of the Wildcard market before deploying it, since as shown in the above code snippet, the result is deterministic.
- (2) can be searched the same way. 


An attacker can find any single address collision between (1) and (2) with high probability of success using the following meet-in-the-middle technique, a classic brute-force-based attack in cryptography:
    
    1. Brute-force a sufficient number of values of salt (2^80), pre-compute the 
       resulting account addresses, and efficiently store them e.g. in a Bloom 
       filter data structure.
    2. Brute-force contract pre-computation to find a collision with any address 
       within the stored set in step 1.

The feasibility, as well as detailed technique and hardware requirements of finding a collision, are sufficiently described in multiple references:

- A past issue on [Sherlock](https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2023-07-kyber-swap-judging/issues/90) and [Code4rena](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-panoptic-findings/issues/482#issuecomment-2096043469) describing this attack.
- [ EIP-3607, which rationale is this exact attack.](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-3607) The EIP is in final state.
- [A blog post discussing the cost (money and time) of this exact attack.](https://mystenlabs.com/blog/ambush-attacks-on-160bit-objectids-addresses)

The [hashrate of the BTC network](https://www.blockchain.com/explorer/charts/hash-rate) has reached `6.5 x 10^20` hashes per second as of time of writing, taking only just 31 minutes to achieve 2^80 hashes. A fraction of this computing power will still easily find a collision in a reasonably short timeline.

**PoC: Draining the market**


Even given EIP-3607 which disables an EOA if a contract is already deployed on top, we show that it's still possible to drain the Wildcard market entirely given a contract collision.

Assuming the attacker has already found an address collision against an undeployed Wildcard market, let's say `0xCOLLIDED`. The steps for complete draining of the market are as follow:

First tx:

Deploy the attack contract onto address `0xCOLLIDED`.
Set infinite allowance for `{0xCOLLIDED ---> attacker wallet}` for any token they want.
Destroy the contract using `selfdestruct`.
Post Dencun hardfork, `selfdestruct` is still possible if the contract was created in the same transaction. The only catch is that all 3 of these steps must be done in one tx.

The attacker now has complete control of any funds sent to `0xCOLLIDED`.

Second tx:

Deploy the market to `0xCOLLIDED`.
Wait until a market deployed holds a significant amount of funds  and drain it.
The attacker has stolen all funds from the market.




**PoC: Detailed steps:**
Here is the PoC, as well as detailed steps to recreate it:

Paste the following file onto Remix (or a developing environment of choice): [POC](https://gist.github.com/midori-fuse/087aa3248da114a0712757348fcce814)
Deploy the contract Test.
1. Run the function `Test.test()` with a `salt` of your choice, and record the returned address. The result will be:
   - `Test.getAllowance()` for that address will return exactly APPROVE_AMOUNT.
   - `Test.getCodeSize()` for that address will return exactly zero.
   - This proves the second property.
2. Using the same salt in step 3, run `Test.test()` again. The tx will go through, and the result will be:
   - `Test.test()` returns the same address as with the first run.
   - `Test.getAllowance()` for that address will return twice of `APPROVE_AMOUNT`.
   - `Test.getCodeSize()` for that address will still return zero.
   - This proves the first property. 

The provided PoC has been tested on Remix IDE, on the Remix VM - Mainnet fork environment, as well as testing locally on the Holesky testnet fork, which as of time of writing, has been upgraded with the Dencun hardfork.


## Impact
Address collision can cause all funds in the wildcard market  to be drain.

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Don't allow the user to control the `salt` used.
2. Consider also adding and encoding `block.timestamp` and `block.number` combined with the user's salt. 


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/WildcatSanctionsSentinel.sol#L96

# Vulnerability details

In `WildcatSanctionsSentinel.sol` , the function `overrideSanction()` and  removeSanctionOverride() are used to overide and remove override of sanction respectively .  There is no access control allowing anyone to call the functions

This allows for race conditions where an attacker can immediately negate a legitimate user's attempt to override their sanction by calling `removeSanctionOverride` right after the user calls `overrideSanction`

## Impact

1. Sanctioned accounts that are not supposed to override sanction their sanction could use `override sanction` to whitelist themselves, allowing them to interact with markets they should be blocked from.

2. Dos as follows :

    - Alice overrides her sanction using the `overrideSanction` function.
    - Bob the attacker monitors for  function  calls of alice and quickly 
      executes the opposite function, `removeSanctionOverride`, to deny Alice 
      access to other features of the protocol. 


## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/WildcatSanctionsSentinel.sol#L96

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/WildcatSanctionsSentinel.sol#L104

## Tools Used
Manual  Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add access control to the `overrideSanction` and `removeSanctionOverride `functions, restricting them to authorized callers  only

DoS

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/klustech/wildcat-vulnerability/blob/main/AccessControlHooks.sol#L13
https://github.com/klustech/wildcat-vulnerability/blob/main/FaultyRoleProvider.sol#L8
https://github.com/klustech/wildcat-vulnerability/blob/main/Exploit.sol#L18


# Vulnerability details

A critical vulnerability was identified in the AccessControlHooks contract of the Wildcat Protocol. The issue stems from the contract's improper validation of credentials returned by external role providers. Specifically, expired credentials returned by the FaultyRoleProvider are improperly accepted by the AccessControlHooks, allowing unauthorized access to privileged functions.

The system relies on external role providers to validate users, and by returning an expired credential, a malicious role provider can bypass the access control check, thus compromising the system's security.



AccessControlHooks deployed to: 0xae314669e3B7E529fDF4da13aF1F1cFFE592031e
FaultyRoleProvider deployed to: 0x5c8D56862E76e9b7f7489f0f3b6E448aCF97CE7A
Exploit deployed to: 0x83973A53C5ed230289C17a9fF4bA2d7f2B79BaE0





## Assessed type

Access Control

brief_summary: The `_transfer()` doesn’t check if the sender or receiver is sanctioned. Neither does the onTransfer hook which enforces access control based on lender credentials but doesn’t check for sanctions. ## Proof of Concept
The idea of `FixedTermLoanHook` is to only allow for withdrawals after a certain term end time. However, the problem is that the current implementation does not look at the expiry, but instead at the `block.timestamp`

```solidity
  function onQueueWithdrawal(
    address lender,
    uint32 /* expiry */,
    uint /* scaledAmount */,
    MarketState calldata /* state */,
    bytes calldata hooksData
  ) external override {
    HookedMarket memory market = _hookedMarkets[msg.sender];
    if (!market.isHooked) revert NotHookedMarket();
    if (market.fixedTermEndTime > block.timestamp) {
      revert WithdrawBeforeTermEnd();
    }
```

This creates inconsistencies such as forcing users not only to wait until term's end, but also having to wait an extra `withdrawalBatchDuration` before they're able to withdraw their funds.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/market/WildcatMarketBase.sol#L665


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Users are incentivized to not withdraw immediately after market is closed.

## Proof of Concept
Within a withdraw batch, all users within said batch are paid equally - at the same rate, despite what exactly was the rate when each individual one created their withdraw.

While this usually is not a problem as it is a way to reward users who queue the withdrawal and start the expiry cooldown, it creates a problematic situation when the market is closed with an outstanding expiry batch.

The problem is that up until the expiry timestamp comes, all new withdraw requests are added to this old batch where the rate of the previous requests drags the overall withdraw rate down.

Consider the following scenario:
1. A withdraw batch is created and its expiry time is 1 year.
2. 6 months in, the withdraw batch has half of the markets value in it and the market is closed. The current rate is `1.12` and the batch is currently filled at `1.06`
3. Now users have two choices - to either withdraw their funds now at `~1.06` rate or wait 6 months to be able to withdraw their funds at `1.12` rate.

This creates a very unpleasant situation as the users have an incentive to hold their funds within the contract, despite not providing any value. 

Looked from slightly different POV, these early withdraw requesters force everyone else to lock their funds for additional 6 months, for the APY they should've usually received for just holding up until now.

## Tools Used
Manual review


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
After closing a market and filling the current expiry, delete it from `pendingWithdrawalExpiry`. Introduce a `closedExpiry` variable so you later make sure a future expiry is not made at that same timestamp to avoid collision.


## Assessed type

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/main/src/access/FixedTermLoanHooks.sol#L413


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
If we look at the code comments, we'll see that role providers can update a user's credential only if at least one of the 3 is true:
- the previous credential's provider is no longer supported, OR
- the caller is the previous role provider, OR
- the new expiry is later than the current expiry

```solidity
  /**
   * @dev Grants a role to an account by updating the account's status.
   *      Can only be called by an approved role provider.
   *
   *      If the account has an existing credential, it can only be updated if:
   *      - the previous credential's provider is no longer supported, OR
   *      - the caller is the previous role provider, OR
   *      - the new expiry is later than the current expiry
   */
  function grantRole(address account, uint32 roleGrantedTimestamp) external {
    RoleProvider callingProvider = _roleProviders[msg.sender];

    if (callingProvider.isNull()) revert ProviderNotFound();

    _grantRole(callingProvider, account, roleGrantedTimestamp);
  }
```

This means that a role providers should not be able to reduce a credential set by another role provider.

However, this could easily be bypassed by simply splitting the call into 2 separate ones:

1. First one to set the expiry slightly later than the currently set one. This would set the role provider to the new one.
2. Second call to reduce the expiry as much as they'd like. Since they're the previous provider they can do that.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Fix is non-trivial.

Context

Title: WildcatArchController contract has Dependence on Predictable Environment Variable in Inherited completeOwnershipHandover Function
•	Severity: Medium

•	Status: Unresolved
•	File: WildcatArchController.sol
•	Lines Affected: 5

WildcatArchController contract has Dependence on Predictable Environment Variable in Inherited completeOwnershipHandover Function.

Issue Title: Dependence on Predictable Environment Variable in Inherited Function
Contract: WildcatArchController
Function Name: completeOwnershipHandover(address) (Inherited from Ownable.sol)
PC Address: 6832
Estimated Gas Usage: 2202 - 2487

The function completeOwnershipHandover is inherited from Ownable.sol in the WildcatArchController contract and is freely callable. This function depends on the block.timestamp environment variable to check whether an ownership handover request has expired. Specifically, the condition if gt(timestamp(), sload(handoverSlot)) is used to validate the expiry of the handover request.

Since block.timestamp is a predictable value that can be manipulated by miners within a small time window, an attacker could leverage this predictability to manipulate the control flow of the ownership handover process, potentially leading to incorrect ownership transfers or disruption in the contract’s ownership logic.

The use of predictable variables like block.timestamp for determining the validity of critical actions (such as ownership handovers) introduces a certain level of trust in miners, which can be exploited in a targeted attack.

Trust in Miners: 
Miners can manipulate block.timestamp within a limited range, potentially altering the outcome of the ownership handover process.

Ownership Takeover Risk:
Attackers could manipulate the block.timestamp to either extend or prematurely expire the ownership handover window, leading to unintended or denied ownership transfers.

Weak Source of Randomness: 
Using environment variables like block.timestamp for decision-making makes the contract vulnerable to manipulation, as these values are easily predictable.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To avoid reliance on block.timestamp or block.number, we can mitigate this issue by using an oracle to provide a more reliable and decentralized source of time, such as Chainlink’s Time Oracle. This ensures the contract is not reliant on environment variables that are susceptible to miner manipulation.

Below is an example of how you could modify the completeOwnershipHandover function to use an oracle service, such as Chainlink’s getTime, instead of block.timestamp:
```sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.4;

import "@chainlink/contracts/src/v0.8/interfaces/OracleInterface.sol"; // Import Chainlink's oracle

contract WildcatArchController is Ownable {
    OracleInterface private timeOracle;  // Define the Chainlink Oracle interface

    constructor(address _oracleAddress) {
        timeOracle = OracleInterface(_oracleAddress);  // Initialize the oracle with the deployed oracle's address
    }

    function completeOwnershipHandover(address pendingOwner) public payable virtual onlyOwner {
        // Query the Oracle for the current time
        uint256 currentTime = timeOracle.getTime();

        // Use the oracle time instead of block.timestamp to check for expiration
        uint256 expiryTime = sload(handoverSlot);

        require(currentTime <= expiryTime, "NoHandoverRequest()");

        // Reset the handover slot after successful ownership transfer
        sstore(handoverSlot, 0);
        _setOwner(pendingOwner);
    }
}
```
Instead of relying on block.timestamp, the function now queries a trusted oracle (e.g., Chainlink’s time oracle) to get the current time via timeOracle.getTime(). This approach eliminates the miner’s ability to manipulate the timestamp, ensuring a more secure and reliable mechanism for validating the ownership handover process.

This implementation assumes the oracle contract provides a getTime() function, which would return the accurate time from an external, decentralized source, safeguarding the process from miner interference.

## Impact
Without verifying the returned data, the system could process invalid or unexpected values, potentially leading to security vulnerabilities or logic errors.

## Proof of Concept
The code checks for the presence of data (returndatasize > 0x1f) and a successful call, but does not validate the actual content of the returned data.

Add a check to validate the content of the returned data before proceeding with further logic.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/WildcatArchController.sol#L87


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
During the review of the updateSphereXEngineOnRegisteredContracts function, it was identified that the address(0) placeholder is used in the addAllowedSenderOnChainCalldata construction. This usage seems incorrect and may lead to misconfiguration or security issues in adding authorized senders.

## Vulnerability Details
The bug stems from the line where abi.encodeWithSelector is used to encode the call to ISphereXEngine.addAllowedSenderOnChain.selector. Instead of passing engineAddress as the parameter, address(0) is used. This would result in trying to add a sender to a non-existent engine address, which could prevent proper function execution. Essentially, the authorization of senders on the SphereX Engine would be skipped, and this could lead to system vulnerabilities or incorrect configurations.

## Impact
If left uncorrected, the system may fail to add the intended addresses to the list of allowed senders on the SphereX Engine. As a result, contracts that rely on the proper authorization of senders will not function as expected, potentially allowing unauthorized transactions or preventing legitimate ones from being processed. This could disrupt the security mechanisms of the protocol.

## Proof of Concept
In the current code:
solidity
Copy code
if (engineAddress != address(0)) {
  addAllowedSenderOnChainCalldata = abi.encodeWithSelector(
    ISphereXEngine.addAllowedSenderOnChain.selector,
    address(0)
  );
}
The issue lies in the address(0) parameter. When executed, it will try to add a non-existent address, resulting in faulty authorization. Replacing address(0) with engineAddress resolves this issue.

## Tools Used
•	Manual code review and analysis.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Replace address(0) with engineAddress in the line that constructs the addAllowedSenderOnChainCalldata variable. The updated code should look like this:
solidity
Copy code
if (engineAddress != address(0)) {
  addAllowedSenderOnChainCalldata = abi.encodeWithSelector(
    ISphereXEngine.addAllowedSenderOnChain.selector,
    engineAddress
  );
}
This will ensure that the correct engineAddress is used when adding authorized senders to the SphereX Engine.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/market/WildcatMarketConfig.sol#L82
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/market/WildcatMarketConfig.sol#L8


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
The WildcatMarketConfig contract currently contains functions, such as nukeFromOrbit, that are not related to configuration but rather to security and account management. These functions are out of place in a configuration contract and should be relocated to a more appropriate contract, such as WildcatMarketSecurity, if necessary.

Additionally, the WildcatMarketConfig contract’s inheritance from WildcatMarketBase seems unnecessary and introduces confusion.

## Vulnerability Details
The WildcatMarketConfig contract is designed to handle configuration settings like total supply, interest rates, and reserve ratios. However, the presence of non-configurational functions like nukeFromOrbit, which involves account blacklisting and sanctions, deviates from the core purpose of the contract.

Additionally, inheriting from WildcatMarketBase is unnecessary for a configuration contract. These issues make the contract less modular, harder to maintain, and potentially confusing for developers who expect it to strictly deal with market configurations.

## Impact
This design issue affects the modularity and clarity of the codebase. By mixing configuration-related logic with account security functions and unnecessary inheritance, the WildcatMarketConfig contract becomes more difficult to understand and maintain.

This could lead to increased complexity when scaling or auditing the contract, as non-related functionalities are bundled together.

## Proof of Concept
The nukeFromOrbit function is a security function that sanctions accounts by transferring balances to an escrow, which has nothing to do with setting market configuration parameters:

solidity

function nukeFromOrbit(address accountAddress) external nonReentrant sphereXGuardExternal {
    if (!_isSanctioned(accountAddress)) revert_BadLaunchCode();
    MarketState memory state = _getUpdatedState();
    hooks.onNukeFromOrbit(accountAddress, state);
    _blockAccount(state, accountAddress);
    _writeState(state);
}
This function should be part of a separate contract focused on security operations, not part of configuration logic.

## Tools Used
Manual code review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Move the nukeFromOrbit function and any other non-configurational functions to a separate contract, such as WildcatMarketSecurity, where account management and sanctions can be handled more appropriately.

The WildcatMarketConfig contract should be strictly used for managing configurational parameters like interest rates, total supply, and reserve ratios, to maintain clarity and modularity.

Also, the inheritance from WildcatMarketBase should be removed to ensure the contract is focused purely on configuration without introducing unnecessary functionality or dependencies.

Governance

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/HooksFactory.sol#L436-L438


# Vulnerability details

### Impact

Protocol plans to support all ERC20 tokens, including those with special names and symbols, but wil not be able to do so for tokens that do not return a string parameter as their name or symbol which will cause market deployment with such assets to always fail.

### Proof of Concept

From the provided informaton in the [readme](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/README.md#general-questions), it can be inferred that all token types are supported. A specific interest is also shown in tokens that return either a bytes32 or a string as their name and symbols. 

> ERC20 used by the protocol	ERC-20s used as underlying assets for markets require no fee on transfer, totalSupply to be not at all close to 2^128, arbitrary mint/burn must not be possible, and name, symbol and decimals must all return valid results (for name and symbol, either bytes32 or a string). Creating markets for rebasing tokens breaks the underlying interest rate model.


However, in HooksFactory.sol, when the `_deployMarket` function is called, the asset's decimal, symbol and name is queried. The name and symbol is then attempted to be concatenated as a string with the name and symbol prefixes. But due to the different parameter types (string prefixes and bytes32 name/symbols), and the attempt to concatenate both as a string, an EVM error will occur, causing the transaction to fail. 

```solidity
    uint8 decimals = parameters.asset.decimals();

    string memory name = string.concat(parameters.namePrefix, parameters.asset.name());
    string memory symbol = string.concat(parameters.symbolPrefix, parameters.asset.symbol());

```

Since a number of tokens including MKR, return a bytes32 name and symbol instead of a string, creating markets for these tokens will always fail going against the protocol's requirements.

### Tools Used

Manual code review
 
### Recommended Mitigation Steps

Fixing this might require using a try-catch to initially query the asset name/symbol, converting the non-string ones to string, before concatenating it with the prefixes.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/HooksFactory.sol#L317-L319


# Vulnerability details

### Impact

Hook deployment is not protected from reorg situations, even though protocol plans on deployment to chains that are very vulnerable to block reorgs. This will cause markets to be deployed with the wrong hooks, messing up users' potential hook configurations.

### Proof of Concept

The protocol plans to deploy on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon. Re-orgs can happen in all EVM chains. Not super common on Ethereum, but still [happens](https://decrypt.co/101390/ethereum-beacon-chain-blockchain-reorg). The same also occurs on Poylgon, which has [experienced large re-orgs in the past.](https://forum.polygon.technology/t/157-block-reorg-at-block-height-39599624/11388) and on Optimistic and Arbitrum rollups.

`_deployHooksInstance` uses the ordinary "create" to deploy the hooks, 

```solidity
      let initCodeSizeWithArgs := add(add(initCodeSize, 0x60), constructorArgsSize)
      // Deploy the contract with the initcode
      hooksInstance := create(0, initCodePointer, initCodeSizeWithArgs)
```
therefore during multiple hook/market deployments through the `deployMarketAndHooks` and `deployMarket` functions, a reorg situation will lead to a "swap" of address instances, in which the reorganization of chain blocks will lead to a different address instance being attached to another hook, other than the one it would have gotten in case of a normal deployment. In short, hook deployment A gets address instance B, rather than address instance A that it would have gotten in case of a normal deployment. 
in case of multiple deployments with the `deployMarketAndHooks` function will cause the wrong hooksinstance to be attached to the wrong markets, which could tamper with various expected market configurations and lead to unexpected behaviour. Also, if the deployer uses the initially derived address and sends funds to the address, the switch in address instance will make the funds open to the other deployment, leading to loss of funds.

### Tools Used
 Manual code review
 
### Recommended Mitigation Steps

Recommend using CREATE2 instead which uses salt that contains msg.sender to deploy hooks instead.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L292-L315


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
The _blockAccount function in the protocol allows a borrower to queue the assets of an account for withdrawal. However, there is no verification to confirm if the account is indeed sanctioned before queuing the assets, which opens up the possibility of arbitrary asset freezes. Even accounts that are not listed on external sanctions (e.g., Chainalysis) can have their assets locked if the borrower triggers the function. This could lead to:
- Borrowers arbitrarily freezing the assets of accounts not on any sanctions list.
- Undermining the intent of the sanctions mechanism, which should only affect sanctioned accounts.

### Vulnerable Code:
The `_blockAccount` function does not check if the borrower’s sanction override is being misused or that the account is even sanctioned at all before queuing an account's assets for withdrawal.
Code link: https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L292-L315
Exploit Scenario:
1. Borrower calls `_blockAccount`, arbitrarily queuing the account’s assets for withdrawal, even though the account is not sanctioned.
2. Financial losses for account holders, as their assets would no longer earn interest while they are queued for withdrawal against their will.
3. Unjust freezing of yield: Even though the account is not sanctioned, it could be prevented from earning the returns it would normally be entitled to (considering the fact that the borrower may no longer needs the credit).

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Add Sanction Verification Before Queuing Withdrawals: The `_blockAccount` function should include a step to check if the account is actually sanctioned, either by external lists or internal rules, before queuing assets for withdrawal. This check should apply regardless of whether the borrower overrides the sanction or not. If no sanctions apply, the account’s assets should not be queued.

2. Add an Appeal or Release Mechanism: Allow users whose accounts have been frozen via `_blockAccount` to appeal the decision or initiate a release request. This would provide protection for innocent users who are unfairly affected.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/WildcatSanctionsSentinel.sol#L26-L28


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
The Wildcat protocol architecture allows borrowers to deploy multiple markets with potentially conflicting sanction rules due to compliance requirements. The current implementation does not handle cases where an account may be sanctioned for one market but not for others, leading to ambiguity in sanction enforcement across multiple markets - deployed by the same borrower. This can result in inconsistent application of sanctions and potential misuse or exploitation by borrowers.

## Impact
This vulnerability can undermine the integrity and effectiveness of the sanction mechanism limiting borrower's specificity on which markets the sanction override should be applied to.

## Proof of Concept
### Code Snippets highlighting vulnerability:
1. Sanction Check Implementation: The `isSanctioned` function in `WildcatSanctionsSentinel` checks if an account is sanctioned but does not account for market-specific overrides.
```solidity
function isSanctioned(address borrower, address account) public view override returns (bool) {
    return !sanctionOverrides[borrower][account] && isFlaggedByChainalysis(account);
  }
```
2. Sanction Override Mechanism: The sanctionOverrides mapping allows borrowers to override sanctions, but it applies uniformly without considering market-specific contexts.
```solidity
mapping(address borrower => mapping(address account => bool sanctionOverride))
    public
    override sanctionOverrides;
```
### Ambiguity Scenario:

1. Borrower deploys two or more markets with different sanction rules (with intension to maintain the sanction in one market and override the sanction in the other market).
2. Borrower overrides a sanction in one market and not in the others.
3. Override applies uniformly without considering market-specific contexts which undermines the agreement that: **A market and its goings-on are between the borrowers and lenders alone**.

## Tools Used
Manual review, VSCode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Modify the sanction override logic to be aware of market-specific contexts and prevent conflicts between different markets.
```solidity
mapping(address borrower => mapping(address market => mapping(address account => bool))) public sanctionOverrides;
```
2. Ensure that all functions that interact with sanctions or overrides account for the market context. This includes modifying `overrideSanction` and `removeSanctionOverride` to take a market address or identifier.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/access/AccessControlHooks.sol#L617


# Vulnerability details

##Proof of Concept

Overview:

The AccessControlHooks contract is designed to enforce access controls on certain market actions like deposits and transfers, ensuring only authorized users can perform them. This is achieved by validating user credentials through role providers. However, there's a critical flaw in how the contract handles the hooksData provided by users during these actions.

Vulnerability Details:

Affected Function: _handleHooksData
Issue: The contract fails to properly validate the length and content of hooksData. If hooksData is empty or shorter than expected, the credential validation process is skipped, allowing unauthorized users to perform restricted actions.
Location in Code:

The vulnerability lies within the _handleHooksData function:

function _handleHooksData(
    LenderStatus memory status,
    address accountAddress,
    bytes calldata hooksData
) internal returns (bool validCredential) {
    // Checks if hooksData contains only a provider address
    if (hooksData.length == 20) {
        // Process hooksData as provider address
        // ...
    } else if (hooksData.length > 20) {
        // Process hooksData with additional credential data
        // ...
    }
    // If hooksData.length < 20, the function does nothing
}


Explanation:

The function checks if hooksData.length is exactly 20 bytes (the size of an address) or greater.
If hooksData.length is less than 20 bytes, the function does not perform any action or validation.
This lack of action means that if a user provides empty hooksData or hooksData shorter than 20 bytes, the contract skips credential validation entirely.
Impact:

An attacker can exploit this vulnerability to bypass the access controls enforced by the contract. By providing insufficient or empty hooksData, an unauthorized user can perform restricted actions such as deposits and transfers without possessing valid credentials.


Step-by-Step Exploitation:

Preparation:
Assume there's a market that uses AccessControlHooks and requires credentials for deposits and transfers.
The attacker does not possess valid credentials and is blocked from performing these actions under normal circumstances.
Crafting Malicious Input:
The attacker calls the onDeposit or onTransfer function of the market contract.
They provide empty hooksData (an empty bytes array) or hooksData shorter than 20 bytes.
Bypassing Validation:
Inside the AccessControlHooks contract, the _tryValidateAccess function is invoked.
_tryValidateAccess calls _tryValidateAccessInner, which in turn calls _handleHooksData.
Since hooksData.length < 20, _handleHooksData does nothing and returns without validating credentials.
The contract fails to set hasValidCredential to false explicitly.
Performing Unauthorized Action:
The attacker proceeds with the deposit or transfer action.
The contract does not enforce the NotApprovedLender error because it mistakenly considers the attacker as authorized.
The unauthorized action is successfully executed.

=> It seems that This vulnerability undermines the entire access control mechanism of the contract and it also allows unauthorized users to participate in restricted markets, potentially leading to financial loss or system abuse.

##Recommended Mitigation Steps

Ensure that hooksData is properly validated for expected length and content before proceeding.
Modify _handleHooksData to revert if hooksData is empty or too short.

In _tryValidateAccessInner, ensure that if no valid credential is found, hasValidCredential is set to false.
Explicitly handle cases where credential validation does not occur due to invalid hooksData.







## Assessed type

Reentrancy

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/market/WildcatMarketBase.sol#L254


# Vulnerability details

##Proof of Concept

A critical vulnerability has been identified in the WildcatMarketBase contract related to the misuse of inline assembly in the _isSanctioned function. This vulnerability allows an attacker to bypass sanction checks, enabling them to interact with the contract even if they are on a sanctions list. The issue arises due to incorrect placement of the function selector and improper alignment of arguments in the assembly code, which leads to malformed calldata being sent to the sentinel contract. 

The vulnerability is located in the _isSanctioned function, which uses inline assembly to call the isSanctioned function on the sentinel contract:

Incorrect Function Selector Placement >
The function selector 0x06e74444 (first 4 bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of isSanctioned(address,address)) is stored at memory address 0x00 using mstore(0, 0x06e74444).
However, mstore writes 32 bytes to memory, and since 0x06e74444 is only 4 bytes, it is stored in the most significant 4 bytes of the 32-byte word, leaving the least significant 28 bytes as zeros.
This misaligns the function selector in the calldata, as the Ethereum ABI expects the function selector to be in the first 4 bytes (least significant bytes) of the calldata.

Function Selector Misplacement:
Incorrect: mstore(0, 0x06e74444)
Stores the 4-byte selector in the most significant bytes of the 32-byte word at address 0x00.
Correct: mstore(0, shl(224, 0x06e74444))
Shifts the selector 28 bytes to the left, placing it in the least significant bytes.


Expected Calldata Layout:

To align with the Ethereum ABI and the EVM's memory model, the calldata should be constructed as follows >

- Bytes 0-3 (most significant bytes): Function selector (4 bytes).
- Bytes 4-35: First argument (borrower).
- Bytes 36-67: Second argument (account).
Note: In EVM memory, the function selector needs to be placed in the most significant 4 bytes of the 32-byte word at the starting memory address.
Actual Calldata Sent:

Due to misalignment, the calldata does not conform to the expected layout, leading to incorrect processing by the sentinel contract.

Note : The Ethereum ABI specifies that the function selector occupies the first 4 bytes of calldata, followed by arguments, each occupying 32 bytes.


Misaligned Arguments>
The first argument _borrower is stored at memory address 0x20 (32 bytes), and the second argument account is stored at 0x40 (64 bytes).
When constructing calldata, the function selector should be immediately followed by the arguments without any padding.
Incorrect Calldata Construction:
The staticcall uses an offset of 0x1c (28 bytes) and a size of 0x44 (68 bytes) for the calldata.
The offset of 0x1c is used to skip the initial 28 bytes of zeros before the function selector.
However, this approach is error-prone and relies on the assumption that the function selector and arguments are correctly aligned after the offset, which may not be the case.
Potential Impact >
Due to the misalignment, the sentinel contract may receive malformed calldata, causing it to either revert or process incorrect data.
If the sentinel contract does not properly validate the calldata, it might return an incorrect result, potentially indicating that a sanctioned address is not sanctioned.
This would allow an attacker on the sanctions list to bypass the checks and interact with the WildcatMarketBase contract.

I haven't time to reproduct it but the reproduction steps can be that : 

- Deploy a Malicious Sentinel Contract:
An attacker deploys a malicious sentinel contract that returns false for any isSanctioned call, regardless of the input.

- The attacker ensures that the WildcatMarketBase contract uses the malicious sentinel contract.
Due to the misaligned calldata, even a legitimate sentinel might not correctly process the sanction check.

- The attacker calls functions on the WildcatMarketBase contract that rely on _isSanctioned for access control.
The misalignment in calldata allows the attacker to bypass the sanction check and perform unauthorized actions.

#Other impacts : 

WildcatMarketWithdrawals inherits from WildcatMarketBase and relies on the _isSanctioned function to perform sanction checks, the misalignment issue in the base contract directly affects the withdrawal contract.

##Recommended Mitigation Steps

Correct Function Selector Alignment:
Ensure that the function selector is placed in the least significant 4 bytes of the first 32-byte word.
Use bitwise shifting to align the function selector correctly.
solidity.

mstore(0, shl(224, 0x06e74444)) // We need to Shift left by 28 bytes to align the selector

We need maybe also to :

- Build the calldata by placing the function selector and arguments consecutively without unintended padding.

- Use a memory pointer to sequentially store the function selector and arguments.


















## Assessed type

Access Control

# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
The function onDeposit and others use calldatacopy to copy additional calldata (extraCalldataBytes) into memory without properly validating its size. This creates a vulnerability where an attacker could send calldata that is larger than expected, resulting in memory corruption as below :
 
let extraCalldataBytes := sub(calldatasize(), DepositCalldataSize);
calldatacopy(
    add(headPointer, DepositHook_ExtraData_TailOffset),
    DepositCalldataSize,
    extraCalldataBytes
);

If extraCalldataBytes is larger than the allocated memory for storing the extra data, it can overwrite critical variables in memory.
For instance, an attacker could send calldata with an excessive payload that overwrites the address of the recipient or modifies other important variables.

Since the code directly interacts with memory at a low level, if extraCalldataBytes is larger than expected, it could overwrite critical variables in memory.

For example, an attacker can send calldata with an oversized payload, leading to an overwrite of sensitive data such as the recipient's address or important state variables.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add a validation step to ensure that extraCalldataBytes does not exceed a reasonable size before copying it into memory :
uint256 MAX_EXTRA_DATA_SIZE = 256; // Define a safe maximum size for extra calldata
require(extraCalldataBytes <= MAX_EXTRA_DATA_SIZE, "extraCalldataBytes exceeds maximum allowed size");

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/types/HooksConfig.sol#L514


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
In several functions like onBorrow, onRepay, and onDeposit, the contract manually constructs calldata using assembly when calling external hook contracts. The issue arises from improper placement of the function selector and incorrect calculation of offsets, leading to misalignment of the calldata.

Example in the onBorrow function : 
- mstore(ptr, onBorrowSelector) stores the 4-byte onBorrowSelector in the most significant 4 bytes of the 32-byte word at ptr, which are bytes ptr + 0 to ptr + 3.
- The least significant 28 bytes (bytes ptr + 4 to ptr + 31) are zeros.

-> The external call uses an offset of add(ptr, 0x1c), which is ptr + 28.
This means the calldata sent to the external contract starts at ptr + 28.
-> This misplacement can lead to the external contract receiving an incorrect function selector.

-> Since the function selector is incorrectly placed in the last 4 bytes of the first 32-byte word, starting the call at this offset misaligns the calldata.


Note : The size of the calldata (size) is calculated incorrectly using RepayHook_Base_Size instead of BorrowHook_Base_Size (Fow now, it is not a problem because it is initialized with the same value).

-> Since the function selector is at ptr + 0 to ptr + 3, starting the calldata at ptr + 28 skips the function selector entirely and starts in the padded area.
-> As a result, the external contract can not receive the function selector, which is essential for identifying which function to execute for exemple.



## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Shift the function selector to occupy the most significant 4 bytes of the 32-byte word (28 to 31).

Context

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/WildcatArchController.sol#L130


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept

In the _updateSphereXEngineOnRegisteredContractsInSet function, the contract checks whether a given address (account) is contained within a specific EnumerableSet.AddressSet (set). If the address is not present, it attempts to revert using a specific error selector provided by notInSetErrorSelectorBytes.

The mstore(0, notInSetErrorSelector) stores the 4-byte error selector at memory address 0x00, in the most significant bytes of the 32-byte word.
The Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) stores values in big-endian format when using mstore, meaning the value occupies the highest-order bytes.
As a result, the error selector occupies bytes 0x00 to 0x03, and bytes 0x04 to 0x1f (up to byte 31) are zero-filled.

The revert(0x1c, 0x04) statement attempts to revert using 4 bytes of data starting from memory offset 0x1c (decimal 28).
However, since the error selector is stored at memory addresses 0x00 to 0x03, the memory from 0x1c to 0x1f contains zeros, not the error selector.

##Impacts 

-> External contracts or applications interacting with WildcatArchController will not receive the intended error selector upon revert and can lead to incorrect application logic or security issues.




## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Store the error selector at memory offset 0x1c (28 bytes), matching the offset used in the revert statement.



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L55-L91
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L146-L166
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/market/WildcatMarket.sol#L168-L177


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept

 **Lack of Zero-Value Checks:**
Functions allow ```amount``` to be zero, enabling no-op transactions or paving the way for exploits.

**Insufficient Balance Checks:**
The contract doesn't verify if users have sufficient balances before borrowing or repaying, potentially leading to negative balances.

**Risk of Underflows/Overflows:**
Without proper arithmetic safeguards, operations on state variables can cause underflows or overflows.

## **Key Functions Reviewed**
#### **Borrow Function**

```solidity
function borrow(uint256 amount) external onlyBorrower nonReentrant sphereXGuardExternal {
    // ... (earlier checks omitted for brevity)

    MarketState memory state = _getUpdatedState();
    if (state.isClosed) revert_BorrowFromClosedMarket();

    + require(amount > 0, "Amount must be greater than zero");
    uint256 borrowable = state.borrowableAssets(totalAssets());
    if (amount > borrowable) revert_BorrowAmountTooHigh();

    // Proceed with borrowing
}
```

#### **Repay Function**

```solidity
function repay(uint256 amount) external {
    + require(amount > 0, "Repay amount must be greater than zero");
    // ... (additional checks omitted)

    // Proceed with repayment
}
```

#### **Deposit Function**

```solidity
function _depositUpTo(uint256 amount) internal virtual nonReentrant returns (uint256 /* actualAmount */) {
    + require(amount > 0, "Deposit amount must be greater than zero");
    // ... (additional logic omitted)

    // Proceed with deposit
}
```

## **Findings**

 **Insufficient Input Validation:**
   - **Issue:** `borrow`, `repay`, and `_depositUpTo` lack checks ensuring `amount > 0`.
   - **Implications:** Enables zero-value operations, risking contract state integrity.

 **Lack of Balance Checks:**
   - **Issue:** No verification of user balances before actions.
   - **Implications:** Potential for negative balances and over-borrowing.

 **Risk of Underflows/Overflows:**
   - **Issue:** Arithmetic operations aren't protected against underflows/overflows.
   - **Implications:** Can lead to incorrect state updates and exploitation.

## **Potential Impact**

- **Financial Loss:** Exploits can manipulate balances, causing discrepancies.
- **Protocol Integrity:** Over-borrowing and negative balances undermine the protocol's reliability.
- **User Trust:** Vulnerabilities erode confidence, potentially reducing user participation and funds.

### **Scenario 1: Borrowing Zero Amount**

**Objective:** Invoke `borrow` with `amount = 0` to bypass restrictions.

**Steps:**
 **Initial State:**
   - `1,000` tokens available.
   - **Borrower A** has no loans.

 **Execution:**
   ```solidity
   borrow(0);
   ```

 **Expected:** Transaction reverts.
 **Actual:** Function executes, possibly emitting misleading events.

**Impact:** Sets precedent for further exploitation.

### **Scenario 2: Exceeding Borrowable Amount via Race Condition**

**Objective:** Borrow more than available by manipulating state between check and transfer.

**Steps:**
 **Initial State:**
   - `1,000` tokens available.
   - **Borrower A** and **Borrower B** active.

 **Execution:**
   - **Borrower A** calls `borrow(1,000)` (check passes).
   - **Borrower B** withdraws `600` tokens before transfer.
   - **Borrower A** receives `1,000` tokens despite only `400` available.

3. **Impact:** Contract holds negative assets (`-600`), violating invariants.

### **Scenario 3: Repaying Excessive Amount Leading to Underflow**

**Objective:** Repay more than debt to cause underflow.

**Steps:**
 **Initial State:**
   - **Borrower A** owes `500` tokens.

 **Execution:**
   ```solidity
   repay(1000);
   ```

 **Expected:** Repayment capped or transaction reverts.
 **Actual:** Debt reduced incorrectly, possible underflow.

**Impact:** Disrupts accounting, enabling debt manipulation.

## **Real-World Relevance**

Similar vulnerabilities have led to significant losses in DeFi protocols:

 **Flash Loan Attacks:** Exploiting input validation gaps to manipulate borrowing limits.
**Negative Balance Exploits:** Causing insolvency by creating negative user balances.

These parallels highlight the necessity of robust input validation to prevent exploitable vulnerabilities.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

**Implement Input Validation:**
   - **Add Checks:**
     ```solidity
     require(amount > 0, "Amount must be greater than zero");
     ```

**Enforce Balance Checks:**
   - **Verify User Balances:**
     ```solidity
     require(userBalance >= amount, "Insufficient balance");
     ```

**Utilize SafeMath Libraries:**
   - **Prevent Underflows/Overflows:**
     ```solidity
     using SafeMath for uint256;
     uint256 newBalance = userBalance.add(amount);
     ```


 **Implement Access Control Mechanisms:**
   - **Restrict Functions:**
     ```solidity
     modifier onlyAuthorized() {
         require(isAuthorized(msg.sender), "Not authorized");
         _;
     }
     ```

 **State Invariant Enforcement:**
   - **Maintain Integrity:**
     ```solidity
     assert(totalBorrowAssets <= borrowableAssets(totalAssets()));
     ```

 **Event Logging for Critical Operations:**
   - **Monitor Activities:**
     ```solidity
     event AssetsLocked(address indexed user, uint256 amount);
     event BorrowConfirmed(address indexed user, uint256 amount);
     ```



## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Borrower creates a market with the `hookTemplate` that was disabled. This may lead to undetermined consequences as it is not intended by the admin.

Borrower creates a market with a hook that was disabled previously via `HooksFactory.disableHooksTemplate()` function

Consider adding a function that allows the owner to enable `hookTemplate`, or implement a check to ensure that the `hookTemplate` is `enabled` when the borrower deploys a market.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/market/WildcatMarketBase.sol#L406-L465
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/libraries/FeeMath.sol#L40-L50


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
According to the docs 
https://docs.wildcat.finance/using-wildcat/protocol-usage-fees

protocolFee is a percent increase in the annual rate that borrower is meant to pay seperate from the annual rate 

using the example in the docs, assuming a protocol fee rate of 5% and annual rate of 10%, the % increase is meant to be 10.5% 
however this condition doesn't hold as protocol rate is calculated as a percentage of (supply + accrued interest) 

example using above rate 
for a supply of 10,000 usdc, the total debt owed after exactly one year should be 10,000 * 10.5 / 100 = 11050 

however due to the way it is calculated 
it will end up being protocolFee 10,000 * 10 / 100 * 0.5 / 100 = 55 
so the borrower would end up paying 11,000 + 55 = 11,055 



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-wildcat/blob/fe746cc0fbedc4447a981a50e6ba4c95f98b9fe1/src/WildcatSanctionsSentinel.sol#L113-L142


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
From the observation of the function using the link below, we can see that the function doesn't implement any restriction to prevent only certain authorised entity to access it. Therefore this can lead to various attack path by a malicious user.

1. Bypassing Sanctions
Sanction Override: Once a user creates an escrow contract for a borrower, that contract becomes a sanction override for that borrower. This means the user can interact with the borrower without restrictions.
Frequent Interactions: The user could engage in multiple transactions with the borrower, effectively bypassing any restrictions intended to prevent such interactions. 
This means that once the contract is created, it can be marked as exempt from any sanctions that would otherwise apply to the borrower's address.

Users could effectively bypass sanctions intended to restrict their financial activities. This could undermine the purpose of the sanctioning mechanism, as the contract they create would be shielded from being blocked or restricted.
Potential Legal Issues:

The integrity of the sanctioning mechanism relies on trust and the ability to enforce restrictions. If users can easily circumvent these rules, it could lead to broader distrust in the platform.

Conclusion
In summary, the ability to create an escrow contract that acts as a sanction override could indeed allow users to interact with other functions in the protocol without the typical restrictions. This highlights the critical need for access controls and proper governance mechanisms to prevent misuse and maintain the integrity of the system.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement access control to this function








## Assessed type

Access Control
